note: A curated subset of CWE weaknesses that matter for an IoT honeypot, each mapped to generic attack family keys (see attack_families.json) so it works across any dataset's labels, not just Edge-IIoTset. The full CWE corpus is 900+ entries, mostly irrelevant here.

items.title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
items.text: The product contains hard-coded credentials such as a password or cryptographic key, used for authentication or encryption. IoT firmware frequently ships with fixed admin accounts that the user cannot change, giving an attacker a dependable way in.

items.title: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
items.text: The product does not perform any authentication for functionality that requires a provable user identity or consumes significant resources. Exposed management interfaces on IoT devices often let anyone issue privileged commands.

items.title: Improper Authentication
items.text: The product does not prove, or incorrectly proves, that an actor is who it claims to be. Weak or bypassable authentication on a device lets an attacker impersonate a legitimate client.

items.title: Weak Password Requirements
items.text: The product does not require that users choose strong passwords, making credentials easy to guess or brute force. Default and simple passwords are the norm across consumer IoT.

items.title: Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default
items.text: The product initializes a resource using a default value that is insecure, such as an open service, a blank password, or a debug account left enabled in shipped firmware.

items.title: Missing Authorization
items.text: The product does not perform an authorization check when an actor attempts to access a resource or perform an action, so a low-privilege or anonymous user reaches functions meant to be restricted.

items.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection)
items.text: The product builds an operating-system command from external input without neutralizing special elements, letting an attacker run arbitrary commands. Common in IoT web panels that shell out to system tools, and the mechanism IoT botnets use to spread.

items.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (SQL Injection)
items.text: The product builds an SQL query from external input without neutralizing it, allowing an attacker to read, modify, or destroy database contents.

items.title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting)
items.text: The product places untrusted input into a web page without proper escaping, so an attacker's script runs in another user's browser. Device admin UIs are a frequent target.

items.title: Improper Input Validation
items.text: The product does not validate, or incorrectly validates, input that affects control flow or data handling. It is the root weakness behind many injection and upload attacks.

items.title: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
items.text: The product lets an attacker upload files of a dangerous type that can be automatically processed or executed, such as a web shell or a malicious firmware image.

items.title: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal)
items.text: The product uses external input to build a pathname without restricting it to a safe directory, letting an attacker read or write files outside the intended location.

items.title: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer
items.text: The product reads from or writes to memory outside the bounds of a buffer. On embedded devices this leads to crashes (denial of service) or remote code execution.

items.title: Out-of-bounds Write
items.text: The product writes data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer, corrupting memory. A classic source of device crashes and takeovers.

items.title: Out-of-bounds Read
items.text: The product reads data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer, often leaking memory contents that aid further attacks or scanning.

items.title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
items.text: The product does not control allocation and maintenance of a limited resource, so an attacker can exhaust CPU, memory, or bandwidth and cause a denial of service. The core weakness behind flooding attacks.

items.title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
items.text: The product allocates a reusable resource on behalf of an actor without limiting how much can be allocated, letting a flood of requests overwhelm the device.

items.title: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
items.text: The product transmits sensitive data in cleartext over a channel an attacker can sniff. Many IoT protocols default to unencrypted transport, exposing credentials and data on the wire.

items.title: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
items.text: The product does not encrypt sensitive data before storing or sending it, so an on-path attacker can read or alter it.

items.title: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
items.text: The product exposes information, such as service banners, versions, or internal details, to an actor not authorized to see it. This feeds reconnaissance, scanning, and fingerprinting.
